correctness.rationale: From the exact almost-perfect identity \((A-1)\sigma(N)=AN-1\) for \(N=p^\alpha q^\beta\), the proper-divisor sum gives \(p,q>A\). Strict finite prime-power abundancy bounds imply positivity of \(D=N[A(p+q-1)-pq]+(p-1)(q-1)\). If the bracket were at most \(-1\), then \(D<0\) because \(N>(p-1)(q-1)\); parity makes the bracket odd, so it is at least one. This is exactly the claimed hyperbola, and the elementary odd-integer spacing argument gives the stated prime bounds. The repository verifier was inspected; its finite checks are corroborative only.

value.rationale: At the first natural support size with two odd primes, the theorem converts a priori unbounded prime choices into an explicit finite region for each binary exponent, independent of the remaining exponents. That is a motivated structural sieve for an existence problem that remains open.
residual_risks: It is a necessary-condition theorem and does not settle existence.

final_claim: If an almost perfect integer has the form \(2^r p^\alpha q^\beta\) with \(r,\alpha,\beta\ge1\) and odd primes \(p<q\), then for \(A=2^{r+1}\) one has \(p,q>A\) and \((p-A)(q-A)\le A(A-1)-1\); hence each fixed \(r\) admits only finitely many possible odd-prime supports, independently of the exponents.
limitations: Necessary conditions only; existence of such three-prime-support almost perfect numbers is not asserted.
The theorem does not bound the exponents \(\alpha,\beta\).
